newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's plan balances budget by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's plan balances budget by 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday will send the Republican-controlled Congress a five-year plan that would balance the budget for first time since 1969, while keeping his priorities for domestic spending.
White House documents obtained by reporters late on Wednesday showed Clinton's plan would take the government from a $126 billion deficit this fiscal year to a $17 billion surplus in 2002.

The formal release of his budget Thursday kicks off what congressional leaders have said they hope will be fruitful bipartisan negotiations on a balanced budget. House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Wednesday: "It would be terrific to have a budget that is not dead on arrival...We think there's a real possibility this is a budget we can work from."
To rousing cheers from both parties at his State of the Union address Tuesday night, the president said Congress has a "historic opportunity" to balance the budget.
But his recommendation that $51 billion be spent to improve education left many Republicans wondering if his budget would reflect a renewed "era of big spending."

His 1998 budget calls for spending $1.69 trillion. The documents showed that if Congress approved his five-year plan, spending through 2002 would be $252 billion less than it would be if current spending and tax policies continued.

Clinton's budget proposed spending $20 billion over five years on new and expanded health care insurance programs for poor children, for children whose parents cannot afford private health insurance and for adults who found themselves between jobs.

In response to criticism that he accepted cuts too deep in welfare programs last year, Clinton recommended $3.3 billion be restored to the food stamps program for the poor, $9.7 billion be added to the Social Security supplemental income program, and $4.9 billion be put back in the Medicaid health program.
As expected, the president recommended $100 billion be saved from the Medicare health program for the elderly and a net $9 billion from Medicaid for the disabled and poor.

Clinton proposed tax cuts of $98 billion over the five years, chiefly aimed at families and those who attend college. It includes a $500 per child credit and $1,500 tax credit or $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition.

More tax incentives for individual retirement savings would be offered and those who make money on sale of a home would not have to wait until age 55 for tax free profit of $500,000. In fiscal 1998 this tax relief would be worth $17 billion to taxpayers.
At the same time, he recommended Congress close many corporate tax loopholes, extend expiring taxes and impose new fees for government services to raise about $76 billion over the five years.

And, to help cut the deficit, the government would raise $36.1 billion from sales of broadcast spectrum, $1.2 billion from sale of Weeks Island strategic petroleum reserves, and $1.4 billion from delay of cost of living increases for retired government workers.
Since the November elections, both sides have declared the end of budget wars that brought the government to a halt in late 1995 and proved extremely unpopular with the public.

Whether they term this budget "alive on arrival" or not will depend on reviews of whether his plan legitimately cuts spending where possible. Republicans have said they will certainly push for larger tax breaks, particularly on profits from investments.

Burson-Marsteller budget analyst Stan Collender said Clinton's plan relied on realistic expectations of the country's economic performance. The White House has been criticized in the past for being overly optimistic.

"This is not an optimistic scenario, or a rosy scenario," Collender said of the forecast for 2.0 percent economic growth in 1997 and 1998. "This is probably right in the middle of the consensus range."

The economy was forecast to strengthen to 2.3 percent growth from 1999 through 2002, still an amount lower than Republicans feel is healthy. White House economists said in the document they expected a 5.3 percent unemployment rate in 1997 and 5.5 percent in 1998. No significant inflation was forecast with a predicted rate of 2.6 percent this year and 2.7 percent in 1998.

A flashpoint in budget negotiations with Republicans, the government's commitment to national defense, would remain relatively stable according to Clinton's plan. Republicans have wanted a defense spending increase of $7 billion.
